title: Paranormal Activity at Theatre Royal Brighton proves the power of horror theatre
excerpt: Paranormal Activity review: Theatre Royal Brighton’s horror play delivers ingenious staging, chilling illusions and powerful scares.
content:
I am going to tell you that Paranormal Activity at the Theatre Royal Brighton is terrifying.

Chances are, you are not going to believe me. 

I imagine you, much like I once did, think that while yes maybe it is very well staged, produced and acted and all of those things, surely a play can't actually be scary in the way a film can. 

You are wrong.

One of the great things about the horror genre is the way that because of its extreme nature, it encourages creators to really push what their mediums are capable of - and Paranormal Activity, which Theatre Royal Brighton kindly offered me tickets to attend, is no different.

The highlight of this show really is its staging and set design, opting for a two-tier dollhouse style view into the lives of couple James and Lou - Americans who have moved to the UK to try and escape the shadow that seems to hang over the latter's head.

The incredible set design was a key part of the experience (Image: Johan Persson)

Jo Castleton stars as a celebrity psychic (Image: Johan Persson)

This being a horror show, I'm sure you can imagine how that works out - although it doesn't all happen quite as you might expect. 

The genius of the staging means that the show is able to brilliantly capture that feeling of walking around your own house late at night, your brain tricking itself into finding threats in every shape in the darkness. With all of it on stage at once, all the time, your growing paranoia is constantly given something to feed off. 

It's supported by some phenomenal sound design. The show isn't afraid to throw some very loud bangs at you, but it's also the subtler moments, the mundanities of everyday life, that draw you into the story and make it feel real. 

This, really, is the strength of horror theatre specifically. The impossible things happening before you - the paranormal activity, you might say - really are happening before you, with no CGI, no camera to misdirect you, just very clever staging, illusions and performances. 

The show's illusions designer Chris Fisher, renowned for a very different kind of magic in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, brings some incredible effects to this show, with one trick in particular causing one of the strongest audience reactions I have ever seen. 

However, the one place this production falls down a little is in the story. 

Hannah Sinclair Robinson and James Bye as Lou and James (Image: Johan Persson)

Caroline Faber was fantastic in her role as a doting mum (Image: Johan Persson)

The script is very strong on a moment-to-moment basis, with only occasional lines feeling clunky or a little too deliberate in their design. 

They are delivered with incredible performances all round from James Bye and Hannah Sinclair Robinson as the beleaguered couple, with fantastic support from Jo Castleton as a celebrity psychic and Caroline Faber as a classic doting American mother.

But, as is so often the case with horror, the show's best moments ultimately lie in its first half, as the paranormal first begins to creep into the normal. For all the breakneck tension that is built throughout, the show's ending did not quite deliver narratively for me. 

I felt we needed a little more payoff for some of the characters, whose personal journeys were unfortunately sacrificed at the altar of scares.

But have no doubt - they are some very effective scares. In my complimentary programme, the show's writer Levi Holloway states: "Good horror doesn't just rob you of sleep, it rules it."

Writing this bleary-eyed the following morning, I'm happy to say he succeeded.
